name: Relative Clauses
summary: Who, which, that, whose and where.

paragraphs: A relative clause gives more information about a noun, using a word such as who, which, that, whose or where. Instead of writing two short sentences, I have a friend. She works in a hospital., you can join them into one: I have a friend who works in a hospital.

Relative clauses are one of the best ways to show grammatical range in IELTS, because they let you build longer, more connected sentences. They also bring some predictable errors, such as choosing the wrong pronoun or adding an extra one. This page covers the forms you need and the mistakes to avoid.

blocks.title: The rule in one line
blocks.text: Who for people, which for things, where for places, whose for possession. Never add an extra pronoun.

paragraphs: Complex sentences are part of the Grammatical Range and Accuracy criterion, and relative clauses are one of the simplest ways to produce them. Used well, they make your writing more fluent and precise.
The common errors, such as which they or who they, are very noticeable to examiners, because they show the sentence was built word by word rather than as one unit.
Each relative pronoun has a clear job. Choosing the right one depends on the noun it refers to: a person, a thing, a place, a time or an owner.

rows: Students who study abroad gain independence.
The policy, which began in 2015, reduced traffic.
The car that I bought is electric.
Workers whose jobs are at risk need retraining.
This is the town where I grew up.
2020 was the year when everything changed.

sections.title: Rule 1: Who for people, which for things
sections.label: Rule 1: Who for people, which for things

paragraphs: The first choice is simple: use who when the noun is a person or a group of people, and which when it is a thing, an animal, an idea or an organization. That can be used for both in many sentences.
Using which for people (students which…) or who for things (a law who…) is a common slip. It does not usually block understanding, but it looks careless.

items.text: Students which study abroad become more independent.
Students who study abroad become more independent.
a policy who protects workers
a policy which (or that) protects workers

blocks.title: Companies
blocks.text: For companies and organizations, which or that is the safer choice in formal writing: companies that invest in training.

sections.title: Rule 2: Do not repeat the pronoun
sections.label: Rule 2: Do not repeat the pronoun

paragraphs: The relative pronoun replaces a word in the clause. Once you use who or which, you must not add he, she, it or they as well, because that would mention the same person or thing twice.
This error is common when learners translate directly from their first language, where the extra pronoun may be normal.

items.text: The students who they live on campus save money.
The students who live on campus save money.
The policy, which it was introduced in 2015, worked well.
The policy, which was introduced in 2015, worked well.
The book that I read it was useful.
The book that I read was useful.

paragraphs: Use whose when the noun owns or has something: a student whose parents are doctors, a country whose economy is growing. Whose replaces his, her, its or their.
A common error is to write who his or who their, which uses two words to do one job.

items.text: Children who their parents work long hours need support.
Children whose parents work long hours need support.
Countries whose populations are aging face new challenges.

sections.title: Rule 4: Where for places, and only places
sections.label: Rule 4: Where for places, and only places

paragraphs: Use where when the clause describes what happens in a place: the city where I was born. Where already means in which or at which.
Do not use where for nouns that are not places, and do not add the preposition again at the end. If you keep the preposition, use which: the town in which I live.

items.text: the village which I grew up
the village where I grew up
the house where I live in
the house where I live
companies where hire young graduates
companies that hire young graduates

paragraphs: A defining clause tells us which person or thing we mean, and the sentence would not make sense without it: Students who cheat should be punished. It has no commas.
A non-defining clause adds extra information about someone or something that is already clear: My brother, who lives in Dhaka, is a doctor. It goes between commas, and you cannot use that in it.

rows: The bus that goes to the airport is cheap.
Dhaka, which is the capital, is very crowded.

items.text: Dhaka, that is the capital, is very crowded.
Dhaka, which is the capital, is very crowded.

sections.title: Rule 6: The verb agrees with the noun before the pronoun
sections.label: Rule 6: The verb agrees with the noun before the pronoun

paragraphs: The verb inside the relative clause agrees with the noun the pronoun refers to. Read back from who, which or that to find that noun before you choose the verb.
This is easy to forget when the clause is long, or when other words sit between the noun and the verb.

items.text: A city that has good transport attracts investors.
Workers who have no training struggle to find jobs.
Countries which has strong economies attract migrants.
Countries which have strong economies attract migrants.

sections.title: Rule 7: When you can leave the pronoun out
sections.label: Rule 7: When you can leave the pronoun out

paragraphs: In defining clauses, you can leave out who, which or that when it is the object of the clause: The book (that) I read was useful. Here, I is the subject, so the pronoun is optional.
You cannot leave it out when it is the subject of the clause. In The students who passed the test…, who is the one doing the passing, so it must stay.

items.text: The course (that) she chose is popular.
The students passed the test received certificates.
The students who passed the test received certificates.

sections.title: Rule 8: Which for a whole idea
sections.label: Rule 8: Which for a whole idea

paragraphs: Sometimes which refers not to a single noun but to the whole idea before it: Prices rose sharply, which caused public anger. In this use, which always comes after a comma, and you cannot replace it with that or what.
This structure is useful in Task 2 for showing results, but use it carefully so the reader knows exactly what which refers to.

items.text: Many people now work from home, which reduces traffic.
Many people now work from home, what reduces traffic.
Many people now work from home, that reduces traffic.

paragraphs: Here is how relative clauses appear in real IELTS writing.

rows: The old factory, which stood by the river, was demolished.
Country A, whose figure was the highest, …
People who exercise regularly live longer.
Cities where public transport is cheap have less traffic.
Many people now shop online, which affects local stores.

paragraphs: These five errors are among the most common relative clause mistakes in IELTS essays.

rows: people who they live in cities
the town where I live in

paragraphs: Use this routine on every relative clause in your final check.

steps: Find each who, which, that, whose and where.
Check the noun it refers to: person → who; thing → which / that; place → where; owner → whose.
Delete any extra he, she, it or they inside the clause.

furtherStudy.title: British Council LearnEnglish Teens: Relative Clauses

cards.front: The doctor ____ treated me was very kind.
cards.why: The doctor is a person, so we use who.

cards.front: The policy, ____ was introduced last year, has reduced traffic.
cards.why: This clause is between commas (non-defining), so that is not allowed.

cards.front: Students ____ parents are teachers often read more.
cards.why: The parents belong to the students, so we use whose for possession.

cards.front: This is the village ____ my grandparents were born.
cards.why: Village is a place, and the clause says what happened there, so we use where.

cards.front: The phone ____ I bought last week has stopped working.
cards.why: Phone is a thing, not a place, so we use that or which.

cards.front: People who ____ in cities often face high rents.
cards.why: Who already refers to people, so we must not add they.

cards.front: Dhaka, ____ is the capital of Bangladesh, is very crowded.
cards.why: The clause is between commas, so we use which, not that.

cards.front: Companies ____ invest in training keep their staff longer.
cards.why: Companies are not places here, so we use that or which.

cards.front: Prices rose sharply, ____ made many people angry.
cards.why: Which can refer to the whole idea before it. What is never used this way.

cards.front: The students ____ passed the exam received a certificate.
cards.why: Who is the subject of the clause (the students passed), so it cannot be left out.
